hints: Start by following the air pathway down Fig. 1.1 from B at the top to M at the tiny air sacs - how does the amount of cartilage change as the tubes get narrower?
Think about why a large airway needs stiff C-shaped rings to stay open, while tiny airways need muscle to control airflow instead of stiff cartilage.
Remember which epithelium is for moving mucus with cilia and goblet cells, and which very thin epithelium is for fast diffusion of gases.
Match each description in Table 1.1 to B for the windpipe, C or J for the airway with cartilage blocks, H for the small airway without cartilage, and M for the air sacs.
walkthrough:
Link Cartilage Type to Airway Size**
Think of cartilage as a support to stop airways collapsing when pressure drops during inhalation. The biggest airway below the larynx is the trachea, labelled B in the centre. It has strong incomplete C-shaped rings. The gap at the back lets the oesophagus expand during swallowing.

Separate Bronchus from Bronchiole**
Air splits at the base of the trachea into the left and right bronchi, labelled C and J. They still need support but are inside the lung, so cartilage is in irregular blocks or plates, not full rings. They are still lined by ciliated epithelium with goblet cells to trap and move mucus up. Smaller branches called bronchioles, labelled H, have no cartilage at all but keep ciliated epithelium and add smooth muscle to control air flow.

Spot the Gas Exchange Surface**
At the ends of the bronchioles are clusters of tiny sacs, labelled M. They are lined by very thin squamous epithelium, one cell thick, with a short diffusion distance and large surface area for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange. That is the alveolus.

Final answer: supported by incomplete (C-shaped) rings - trachea - B; lined by ciliated epithelium + blocks of cartilage - bronchus - C (J acceptable); lined by squamous epithelium - alveolus/alveoli - M (D acceptable); lined by ciliated epithelium but no cartilage - bronchiole - H.

hints: Sort the five statements into three groups - one about genes and cancer, two about heart and circulation, and two about breathing and blood gases.
Recall which gas binds strongly to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin and lowers oxygen transport.
Recall which sticky mixture irritates airways and stimulates goblet cells, and which general word describes any chemical that causes DNA mutation leading to uncontrolled division.
Think about which addictive stimulant drug acts on the nervous system to speed up the heart and constrict arterioles in the short term.
Check that B and E share the same stimulant, while A, C and D each need a different term: mutagen/carcinogen, carbon monoxide and tar.
walkthrough:
Mutation of Cell Cycle Genes**
Chemicals that damage DNA and cause mutations in proto-oncogenes or tumour suppressor genes are called mutagens. Because they can lead to cancer they are also called carcinogens. Tobacco smoke contains many, such as tar chemicals and benzo[a]pyrene. That matches A.

Stimulant Effects on Heart and Vessels**
Nicotine is absorbed into blood and stimulates the nervous system. It causes adrenaline release, so heart rate increases and arterioles constrict, giving a short-term rise in blood pressure. That is why both B and E are nicotine.

Oxygen Transport and Mucus**
Carbon monoxide binds to the same site on haemoglobin as oxygen but much more strongly, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. This reduces the oxygen carrying capacity of blood. That matches C. Tar is the sticky particulate mixture that irritates the airways, paralyses cilia and stimulates goblet cells to produce more mucus, leading to smoker's cough and chronic bronchitis. That matches D.
Final answer: A - mutagen / carcinogen; B - nicotine; C - carbon monoxide; D - tar; E - nicotine.
